D.treatment: successive testing of the same individuals

O.outcome_detail: constancy of IQ across successive testing up to age 14

cells.quote: Terman and Stern have found, however, by successive testing of the same individuals that I Q's gotten by dividing mental by chronological age do remain fahly constant up to the age of 14
cells.note: The study reports this finding as a citation to Terman and Stern; it gives no comparison condition, statistical effect size, or details of the participants' setting or testing interval.

cells.quote: These superior and average children develop at different levels and grow increasingly dissimilar with age.
cells.note: Observed comparison of groups defined by mental-growth status; no instructional treatment was manipulated.

cells.quote: The superior children show this acceleration about one year earlier than the average children.
cells.note: The contrast concerns naturally occurring learner groups, not an instructional intervention.

cells.quote: The mean mental age of physiologically accelerated children is higher than for physiologically retarded children when those above the norm in height and weight (the accelerated) are compared with those above the mean mental age for each year.
cells.note: The study reports an observed association between physiological maturity and mental age.

O.outcome_detail: stability of relative IQ position over approximately four years

cells.quote: The coefficient between the first IQ and the fifth IQ is +0.82 for the boys and girls, which indicates that they keep their relative positons after an interval of approximately 4 years.
cells.note: Repeated Stanford-Binet examinations were used; this is a longitudinal association, not a manipulated treatment comparison.

cells.quote: He shows conclusively that it is fairly constant though subject to fluctuations so far as the measurements made are reliable.
cells.note: No study text is available; this quote is copied from the wiki entry.

cells.quote: He has also pointed out that the results of repeated examinations exhibit a definite practice effect.
cells.note: No study text is available; this quote is copied from the wiki entry. The entry does not report an effect size or test statistic.

O.outcome_detail: successful or average first-year high-school work

cells.quote: The Providence table would seem to indicate that in order to do successful work in the first year of high school, an intelligence quotient of 120 is necessary. Terman would predict average high school success where the intelligence quotient is 110.
cells.note: This is a comparison of intelligence-level estimates, not a manipulated educational treatment.

O.outcome_detail: median intelligence quotient in the twelfth year

cells.quote: In the twelfth year, where the discrepancies are the greatest, the median child in the lowest scoring group has an IQ of 0.93, and the median child in the highest scoring group has 1.04 for an IQ.
cells.note: The study reports descriptive IQ values, not an effect size or inferential test.

O.outcome_detail: intelligence quotients on group and individual examinations

cells.quote: The authors have found for example, that in the foreign section of a city where the adults are engaged mostly in unskilled or semi-skilled labor the intelligence quotients on both group and individual examinations are likely to run low.
cells.note: The comparison group and numerical effect are not specified; this is an observational report.

cells.quote: The following year, 1920, brought a queer slump in his record. He was then 7 years 9 months old but tested only 7-2, which caused his IQ to drop to 94. In this test he failed three tests which he had passed the previous year, and he was not given the chance to make points on the form board as previously. Had he passed these four his IQ would have been 101.
cells.note: Single-child longitudinal case comparison; the study attributes the lower 1920 IQ largely to failures on previously passed tests and a different opportunity to earn form-board points.

D.comparison: failure to put forth full effort during testing

cells.quote: It seems reasonable to suppose that the lower IQ's resulting from the first examinations were due to the failure of the subject to put forth his full effort during the testing. The fact that each year he did better on other examinations is evidence in support of this supposition.
cells.note: Case analysis of pupil 24; the study presents a narrative attribution rather than a manipulated effort condition.

D.treatment: greater command of English after 15 months
D.comparison: limited English command at first test

cells.quote: It seems reasonable to suppose that the difficulties which he experienced on the first examination were largely linguistic. As he gained a greater command of English he was able to pass more of the tests, and so made a higher mental age.
cells.note: Case 49 was first tested at age 5 years 9 months and retested 15 months later; most first-test failures were linguistic.

O.outcome_detail: change in IQ score over 6 months to 3 years

cells.quote:
It will be seen, on inspection, that these subjects as a group did not deteriorate.
The average change is an increase of + 1.28.
cells.note: The study reports a descriptive increase but prints no significance test or interval, so the direction is coded ? rather than +.

O.outcome_detail: variability and constancy of IQ change

cells.quote: It is significant that the curve does not differ from the one worked out by Terman from the records of unselected school children. ("The Intelligence of School Children,'1 p. 141 ff.) The indication is that mental defectives are not more variable than normal subjects.
cells.note: The comparison is with Terman's records of unselected school children rather than a randomized concurrent comparison; no test statistic, effect size, power analysis, or equivalence test is printed.
